crime: Craftwork was a permitted pastime — scraps of cloth and cord, small tools kept in the cells with the warden's leave. Hers was the only cell with one girl in it. The friend came every evening after supper and the two worked together; the friend left her box and half-made pieces there between evenings.

For a week the friend had spent her evenings in another girl's cell instead. That day the friend carried her box out, down the corridor to that girl's, and left the half-made pieces behind. Twice that week the friend and that girl had been heard arguing over cord taken from the friend's unfinished work.

She almost never borrowed. That afternoon she asked for the other girl's craft-knife in front of others — a strap of her own to mend. After supper, within earshot, she told the friend she would carry the remaining pieces up to the library before lock.

She carried the pieces up to the library, where near half past nine the friend was crouched over them. From behind she took the friend by the hair and opened her throat with the borrowed blade, and held her there until the friend stopped moving. She left the blade beside the friend and went down before lock with empty hands.
In the morning the other girl found the blade among her things, bloodied. The girls found the friend in the library, the half-made pieces beside her.
Before the court she said she had taken the pieces up and left the friend alive, and returned the knife to its owner that afternoon.

The other girl had stood in the shower queue at the hour of the killing. At ten the doors were locked from the outside, each girl shut in her own cell until the dawn unlocking. Inside hers the other girl turned out her craft box for the knife while her cellmate watched, and there was none.

The girls who had ever handed her anything of theirs were asked one by one, and none had told another before. Each said the same: what they handed her was back with them by morning, unseen, gone out of her hands from wherever she had left it. The blade went back that night — it was in her keeping when it was used.
fields.epitaph: She always knew that people go. In the end, so did everything she held.
execution: An iron frame stood on its own iron base, a crossbar spanning the top. At the warden's order every girl of the court put a strap of her own into her hands; those straps were tied around her — each at one end to a peg on the crossbar — and held her close beneath the bar, the full height of the frame between her and the base.
Through the hour the straps left their pegs one at a time, and the girls on the benches found them in their own hands.
The harness thinned; her weight shifted onto what remained.
The last strap was in its lender's hands, and nothing held her. She fell the height of the frame and struck the iron base.

magic.name: Back by Morning
magic.text: Whatever its owner hands over to her returns to that owner by morning, on its own and unseen.
